title: Why Motivation Theories in Education Haven't Changed in Decades (And Why It Matters for Schools)
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick summarizes a new Educational Psychologist paper by Kou Murayama and Luise von Keyserlingk that asks why the same motivation theories -- self-determination theory, expectancy-value theory, achievement goal theory -- have dominated educational psychology for over 40 years with little fundamental change. The authors' core critique is that these theories describe what motivates students (mastery goals, self-efficacy, need satisfaction) without explaining how motivation actually operates mechanistically, which means the theories 'bend but never break' under contradictory evidence and offer little guidance for why motivation interventions so often fade out over time. As an alternative, the paper proposes a 'reward-learning framework': students become aware of a knowledge gap, that awareness triggers information-seeking, learning becomes intrinsically rewarding, and new knowledge generates further questions, creating a self-sustaining engagement loop. Hendrick translates this into four practical takeaways for teachers -- surface knowledge gaps deliberately, make feedback loops visible, think in longer timescales, and stop labeling students as simply 'high' or 'low' motivation -- and closes with his own long-held view that motivation is more often a side effect of competence and achievement than something to be directly induced.
points: The paper's central critique -- that motivation theories explain what predicts good outcomes without explaining the mechanism -- gives Hendrick a concrete diagnosis for why motivation interventions reliably 'fade out' after initial gains.

The proposed 'reward-learning framework' reframes motivation as a self-sustaining cycle (knowledge gap awareness leads to information-seeking leads to reward leads to new questions) rather than a static trait to be boosted with external interventions.

Hendrick's practical translation asks teachers to deliberately surface knowledge gaps and make feedback loops visible to students, rather than relying on generic appeals to intrinsic motivation or external rewards.

His closing claim -- that motivation is often a side effect of achievement rather than a precondition for it -- inverts the common instinct to 'motivate first, then teach,' suggesting competence-building itself is the more reliable motivational lever.
quotes: Why have the same motivation theories dominated education for decades with so little change?
these frameworks have dominated educational psychology for 40+ years.
they identify what motivates students without adequately explaining how motivation actually works at a mechanistic level.
The theories bend but never break under the weight of contradictory evidence.

to understand and prevent the fade-out effect, the field needs to understand the mechanisms by which interventions promote students' engagement, preferably explanations of how their motivation can be sustained for a long period of time.
in order to motivate students, don’t try and motivate them. Motivation often is a side-effect of other things like achievement rather than being ‘motivated.
